newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Analysts flat on UBS 1996 results.
newsitem.headline: Analysts flat on UBS 1996 results.

text.p: Analysts said they saw no reason to revise recommendations on Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) after the group reported 1996 results.

UBS reported a loss of 348 million Swiss francs, less than a loss of about 500 million it forecast last November due to a one-time charge of three billion Swiss francs to cover bad Swiss domestic loans.

Madeleine Hofmann at CS First Boston Equity Research said she was disappointed at costs, which were driven higher by a 17-percent rise in personnel costs from performance and profit-related bonuses due to lucrative trading business.
"Cash-flow was only better than I estimated because taxes were lower. That means the operating result was worse than I expected," Hofmann said.
Hofmann said the cost to operating income ratio, which she uses as a benchmark of operating performance, was worse than expected at 67.1 percent. She had forecast 65.2 percent.
"I believe I will maintain a hold (recommendation) but I am certainly not more positive than before," she said.
Analysts had recently predicted the loss would be less than the 500 million Swiss francs forecast by the bank late last year. Hofmann had estimated the loss at 351 million.
Hofmann said she would now revise her forecasts for 1997 and 1998 but did not expect to make any major changes.
She currently sees net profit at 2.47 billion Swiss francs this year and 2.84 billion in 1998, with EPS at 96.2 Swiss francs in 1997 and 110.9 next year.
John Leonard at Salomon Brothers in London also said he expected to maintain his hold rating.
"Expenses were a little higher than expected. But basically the report did not come up with much new insight into the company," Leonard said.

Leonard said high bonuses for investment bankers and traders were an issue for most banks, aggravated for Swiss banks by the fact that much of these staff are paid in dollars or sterling, which rose against the Swiss franc last year.
UBS was also aggressively hiring investment banking talent in the United States in an effort to expand there, forcing them to offer generous compensation packages to match a competitive market.
"My forecast is about 2.3 billion Swiss francs (1997 net profit) and I think I'm about the middle of the range," he said.
Leonard expects net profit of 2.5 billion Swiss francs in 1998, with EPS around 91 Swiss francs in 1997 and 96.9 next year.

Analysts mostly agreed with UBS that an extraordinary provision of three billion Swiss francs and ordinary provisions of 1.4 billion for bad domestic loans would be enough to solve the problem of mounting Swiss credit risk.
"The extraordinary provision is based on a realistic evaluation of the economic situation," said Christoph Bieri from Zurich Cantonal Bank.
Bieri was one of the few recommending UBS as a buy, with net profit forecast at 2.7 billion Swiss francs and 2.95 billion in 1998. He sees EPS at 106 Swiss francs this year and 115 next year.
Claudia von Tuerk at Pictet & Cie in Geneva said her outlook for 1997 was far above a minimum goal of two billion Swiss francs named by UBS chief executive Mathis Cabiallavetta.

"They have a huge basis effect given the fact that 1996 ordinary provisions were about 1.4 billion and in 1997 there are going to be -- from what they said -- somewhere between 400 and 600 million," she said.
"All things being equal, we are talking about another billion flowing through, with an impact on taxes of course," she added.
Von Tuerk said she did not expect to change her hold recommendation. -- Zurich Newsroom, +41-1-631 7340
